title: Edit Distance
description: Brute force to optimized: unmemoized recursive exploration of all three operations versus a 2D bottom-up DP grid.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given two words word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations (insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character) required to convert word1 into word2.

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Minimum operations (insert, delete, replace) to transform one string into another\"","The classic edit distance 2D DP: matching characters skip diagonally for free, mismatches cost 1 plus the best of the three neighboring sub-problems"]]}

blocks.text: Define dp[i][j] as the minimum edit operations to convert the first i characters of word1 into the first j characters of word2. If the LAST characters match, no operation is needed for them, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (skip diagonally for free). If they do NOT match, one operation must be spent, corresponding to either replacing (dp[i-1][j-1]), deleting from word1 (dp[i-1][j]), or inserting into word1 to match word2 (dp[i][j-1]), taking the CHEAPEST of these three options.

blocks.title: Analogy: Correcting a Rough Draft Into a Final Document With the Fewest Edits
blocks.text: Picture editing a rough draft into a final document, allowed to insert, delete, or replace individual characters, wanting the fewest total edits. Wherever the current ending characters of both versions already match, no edit is needed there; otherwise, the cheapest of three possible single edits (replace, delete from the draft, or insert to match the final) is chosen.

blocks.caption: Matching characters skip diagonally for free; mismatches cost 1 plus the best of insert, delete, replace

blocks.text: Result: 3 (replace 'h' with 'r', delete 'r', delete 'e': "horse" to "rorse" to "rose" to "ros").

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: dp[i][0] = i (deleting all i characters of word1 to reach an empty word2 prefix), and dp[0][j] = j (inserting all j characters to build up word2 from an empty word1 prefix).

Observation 2: If word1[i-1] equals word2[j-1] (the last characters of the current prefixes match), no new operation is needed for this position, so dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1].

Observation 3: If they do NOT match, exactly one operation must be spent here: REPLACE (dp[i-1][j-1] plus 1), DELETE from word1 (dp[i-1][j] plus 1), or INSERT into word1 (dp[i][j-1] plus 1); dp[i][j] takes the smallest of these three options.

Observation 4: Filling this grid row by row builds the final answer at dp[m][n].
This leads to a 2D bottom-up DP grid, with the first row/column as base cases, and each other cell taking the diagonal (on a match) or the minimum of three neighbors plus 1 (on a mismatch).
Recursively try all three operations (insert, delete, replace) at every position where characters mismatch, without memoization.
Why the code is written this way

items: Trying all three operations recursively directly implements the definition.
This recomputes the same (i, j) sub-positions repeatedly across different operation sequences, costing exponential time; a 2D DP grid computes each sub-position exactly once.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(3 raised to max(m,n)) without memoization.
Space: O(m+n) recursion depth.
Limitation: a 2D DP grid computes each (i, j) sub-position exactly once, reusing smaller sub-positions directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a (m+1) by (n+1) DP grid. Set dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j (base cases). For i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n: if word1[i-1] equals word2[j-1], set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] (free skip); otherwise, set dp[i][j] = 1 + min(dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (the cheapest of replace, delete, insert). Return dp[m][n].
Use a 2D bottom-up DP grid, skipping diagonally on a match, or taking 1 plus the minimum of three neighbors on a mismatch.

blocks.text: The base cases correctly capture the trivial "convert to/from an empty string" scenarios (needing exactly as many inserts or deletes as remaining characters); for every other cell, matching last characters need no operation (free diagonal skip), while a mismatch is correctly resolved by trying all three possible single operations and taking whichever leads to the smallest already-computed sub-problem, guaranteeing the global minimum by the time dp[m][n] is reached.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(m times n).
Space: O(m times n), reducible to O(min(m,n)) using a rolling row.

blocks.text: Edit Distance is one of the most iconic 2D string DP problems, forming the basis of real-world tools like spell checkers and diff algorithms.

blocks.text: If the interviewer says "minimum operations (insert, delete, replace) to transform one string into another", think: a 2D DP grid combining diagonal, top, and left neighbors.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The unmemoized recursive approach costs O(3^max(m,n)); the 2D DP grid costs O(m times n), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: 2D bottom-up dynamic programming comparing two strings character by character.
Core Idea: matching characters skip diagonally for free; mismatches cost 1 plus the best of replace, delete, insert.
Time: O(3^max(m,n)) for the brute force, O(m times n) for the DP approach.
Space: O(m+n) recursion depth for the brute force, O(m times n) (reducible to O(min(m,n))) for the DP approach.
Most Important Observation: a character match is a free diagonal skip, never an operation.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, classic hard-tier DP problem.
One line memory trick: match skips free; mismatch costs 1 plus the best neighbor.
